title: Black Hawk Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Black Hawk wells have a 275 ft median depth, with local drilling and finished-well costs shaped by fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: Black Hawk Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land around Black Hawk means dealing with mountain bedrock, not a predictable shallow aquifer. Permit records within five miles show a 275-foot median well depth, a typical reported yield near 7 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 70 feet below ground.

Those figures are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a new hole will find. Most permitted wells identify an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, and nearby results can vary sharply over short distances. Records from Black Hawk, Central, Idaho Springs, and the surrounding mountain corridors are a starting point for a site-specific drilling, septic, and building decision.

sections.heading: Black Hawk well depth is controlled by fractured bedrock
sections.html:
The middle half of reported wells near Black Hawk runs from 160 to 402 feet. That is a broad range for estimating a bid. A driller who prices only a shallow hole may leave you exposed to added footage, casing, grout, access work, or difficult drilling in granite and gneiss.

Depths are spread across the records: 13% are under 100 feet, 40% fall from 100 to 300 feet, and 37% run from 300 to 600 feet. Another 10% exceed 600 feet, with the deepest recorded well at 1,401 feet. The 90th percentile is 600 feet, so a bid should explain its footage allowance and the price for drilling beyond it.

sections.heading: What a Black Hawk well may produce
sections.html:
Among the wells that report pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 4.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. That is generally a workable range for ordinary household planning, but the yield test and storage system matter more than a regional median for a particular home.

The records show 64% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 28% fall between 1 and 5. Only 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, and 7% report more than 15. Ask for the well-completion report, test duration, recovery information, and proposed tank size. A good short-term flow rate does not by itself prove dependable long-term supply.

sections.heading: Water levels around Black Hawk need a closer look
sections.html:
The median static water level is 70 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 40 to 100 feet. That affects pump setting, electrical load, and the amount of water available above the pump. It also helps a contractor estimate the finished system, although a water level can change with season, recharge, nearby pumping, and the exact fracture system.

The decade series does not show a simple one-way decline. Median depth to water was 38 feet in the 1970s, 90 feet in the 2010s, and 60 feet in the 2020s. The older and newer measurements are not a substitute for a current site test. Compare nearby completion reports and have the driller measure the new well after construction.

sections.heading: Black Hawk’s permit history shows where experience is concentrated
sections.html:
The records include 2,784 permitted wells within five miles, with 1,862 recorded as constructed. Permit activity was strongest in the 1970s, with 616 permits, and the newest permit year is 2025. The use mix is mainly domestic or household at 84%; monitoring wells account for 10%, while stock accounts for 2%.

Three names appear most often in the drilling records: C. R. Smith Drilling with 543 records, C R Smith Drilling Inc with 329, and James Drilling Company with 138. These are record counts, not endorsements. Confirm current licensing, insurance, access capability, and the exact scope of any proposal before choosing a contractor.

sections.heading: A Black Hawk well budget starts with the footage
sections.html:
In this fractured mountain ground, the drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 275 feet, the drilled hole models to about $17,900 to $27,500. That is not the complete water-system price.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical models to about $23,900 to $39,500. Access for a rig, difficult formations, extra casing or grout, water testing, and site restoration can change the proposal. Ask whether the bid covers mobilization, a dry or low-yield hole, casing, development, pump installation, and connection to the house. On a mountain lot, driveway and utility access can be as important to the final price as the hole itself.

sections.heading: Mine features, septic layout, and low-yield risk
sections.html:
Mountain wells can be unpredictable because water travels through fractures rather than a uniform sand or gravel layer. The mapped area has 3,577 historic mine features, 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles. Those records do not establish contamination on a specific parcel, but they justify a careful water-quality review and laboratory testing.

Before building, check the well permit, completion report, setback requirements, and septic feasibility. A low-yield well may need storage and careful household demand planning. A dry hole is a real financial risk, so understand the drilling contract before work starts. DWR permit conditions, household-use limits, augmentation requirements in over-appropriated basins, and county septic approval all need to be reviewed for the intended use.

sections.heading: What to do before buying a Black Hawk lot
sections.html:
Start with the neighboring well records, not with a promised number from a listing. Compare depth, reported yield, static water level, aquifer description, permit use, and the age of each completion report. The local records are dominated by unnamed fractured-bedrock wells, with 2,706 entries; only 15 name a Fractured Crystalline aquifer and 11 name Fractured Granite. There are no Denver Basin aquifer wells in this dataset.

For a purchase, make the well inspection and water-quality testing part of due diligence. For vacant land, obtain a driller’s access and footage estimate, confirm a legal building and septic area, and budget the complete system rather than drilling alone. Central is about one mile away, Idaho Springs about four, and St. Mary’s about eight, but distance to a nearby community does not replace parcel-specific geology or permitting review.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Black Hawk, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Black Hawk is 275 feet. The middle half runs from 160 to 402 feet, while 10% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,401 feet. Because most wells use fractured mountain bedrock, nearby wells can differ substantially in depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Black Hawk?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 275-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $17,900 to $27,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $23,900 to $39,500. Access, casing, grout, and difficult drilling can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Black Hawk well produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 7.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 4.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. About 64% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. These are regional records, not a guarantee for a new well. Request the completion report and test details for the specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Black Hawk, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. The area includes 13 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3,577 historic mine features, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about ten miles. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby land uses, mine history, and the well’s construction records.

faq.q: Is Black Hawk well water getting deeper?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a simple one-way trend. Median depth to water was 38 feet in the 1970s, 90 feet in the 2010s, and 60 feet in the 2020s. Only 183 wells report static water level, so the series is limited. A current measurement and nearby well comparison are more useful for a purchase decision.
